prompt: How did the non-word "dord" get into Webster's New International Dictionary in 1934?
options: A slip reading "D or d", abbreviations for density, was mistaken for one word
An editor planted it to catch copycat dictionaries
A printer misspelled the word "door"
It was an old dialect word for density that had died out
correctAnswer: A slip reading "D or d", abbreviations for density, was mistaken for one word
explanation: Headword slips were typed with spaces between the letters, so "D or d" looked like one spaced-out word. An editor caught it in 1939, but it stayed in print until 1947.

prompt: Lillian Virginia Mountweazel, the mailbox photographer in the 1975 New Columbia Encyclopedia, was a real artist whose entry simply contained errors.
explanation: She was invented, down to her death at 31 on assignment for Combustibles magazine. One of the editors said a fake entry was an old encyclopedia tradition for protecting copyright.

prompt: The made-up word planted in the 2001 New Oxford American Dictionary, defined as "the willful avoidance of one's official responsibilities", is __________.
explanation: Shown six suspicious words, seven of nine experts picked it out. The editors wanted a word that could not arise in nature, and even its "l" has no linguistic reason to be there.

prompt: Which word, left out of "Buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo", marks where a relative clause begins?
options: that
and
the
then
explanation: English lets you drop "that" from a relative clause, as in "Mice cats chase eat cheese". Put it back and the sentence reads: Buffalo buffalo [that] Buffalo buffalo buffalo, buffalo Buffalo buffalo.

prompt: Match each invention to where it appeared:

pairs.right: Webster's New International Dictionary, Second Edition (1934)
A 1930s road map of New York State

explanation: Only dord was an accident. The others were planted on purpose, because a copier can rediscover a real fact but never a fake one.

prompt: Which feature did Daniel Everett claim the Pirahã language lacks, in a challenge to Noam Chomsky?
options: Recursion: putting a phrase inside another of the same type
Vowels
Verbs
Any fixed word order
correctAnswer: Recursion: putting a phrase inside another of the same type
explanation: Everett said Pirahã strings short sentences instead, such as "I saw the dog. The dog was at the beach." Critics found embedded clauses in his own earlier data, and a 2016 corpus study called its own results highly tentative.

prompt: Guugu Yimithirr has no words at all for a person's left and right hands.
explanation: It has them, and it distinguishes left-handedness from right-handedness too. What it does not do is say where things are by left and right: it uses four compass roots, gungga, jiba, naga and guwa.

prompt: The English word kangaroo comes from the Guugu Yimithirr word __________, written down by James Cook's crew in 1770.
explanation: Cook's journal for 4 August 1770 calls the animal "Kangooroo, or Kanguru". The story that the word meant "I don't understand" is a myth.

prompt: Which familiar kind of consonant is missing from Rotokas altogether?
options: Nasals, such as m and n
Stops, such as p and k
Sounds made with the lips
Sounds made with the back of the tongue
correctAnswer: Nasals, such as m and n
explanation: With only six consonants, Rotokas sits at the very bottom of the World Atlas of Language Structures survey. Pirahã also makes no systematic use of nasal sounds.

prompt: Match each language to what makes it unusual:

pairs.right: No word for any exact number, not even one
Places things by compass direction, never by left and right

explanation: Consonant counts run from Rotokas's 6 to !Xóõ's 122, with a typical language in the low twenties; English has 24.

prompt: In the standard description of Silbo Gomero, the whistled Spanish of La Gomera, how are the five Spanish vowels whistled?
options: With two distinct whistles
With five different whistles, one per vowel
With one whistle per letter of the alphabet
They are left out entirely
explanation: Two vowel whistles and four consonant whistles, told apart by pitch and by whether the whistle is continuous or broken. With so few sounds, words like gallina (hen) and ballena (whale) sound alike, and context decides.

prompt: African talking drums work like Morse code: each message is a pre-arranged pattern of beats with no link to spoken words.
explanation: The drums copy the high and low tones of real words in tonal languages, so drum language is essentially the spoken language. Long stock phrases make each word's tone pattern unique.

prompt: On the Lokele talking drums, the moon is never drummed as a single word but as the phrase "the moon looks down at the __________".
explanation: Many Kele words share the same tones, so drummers wrap each one in a phrase with a unique pattern. Money, for example, is "the pieces of metal which arrange palavers".

prompt: What did a 2024 study of historical, demographic and family records conclude about the signing community of Martha's Vineyard?
options: It began in Chilmark around 1785 and had only about 40 years of independent development
It was isolated from all other sign languages for more than 300 years
It never included any hearing people
It was invented by Alexander Graham Bell in the 1880s
correctAnswer: It began in Chilmark around 1785 and had only about 40 years of independent development
explanation: The study puts its start 93 years later than earlier accounts. From the 1820s deaf islanders were schooled on the mainland, linking the island to the young New England signing community.

prompt: Match each term to what it describes:

pairs.right: Yoruba drum whose pitch rises as its cords are squeezed
A longer drum phrase that gives a word a unique tone pattern
A sign language used by deaf and hearing people in one small community

explanation: Whistles, drums and hands can all carry a language. Whistles and drums copy the sounds of speech, while village sign languages such as the Vineyard's are languages of their own.

prompt: Where and how did OK first appear in print, in March 1839?
options: In the Boston Morning Post, as a joke abbreviation of "oll korrect"
In a Choctaw treaty, as the word okeh
On papers signed by Andrew Jackson
On a campaign banner for Martin Van Buren
correctAnswer: In the Boston Morning Post, as a joke abbreviation of "oll korrect"
explanation: It was one of many comic abbreviations of misspellings in the Boston papers, alongside O.W. for "oll wright". The Van Buren link came a year later, in the 1840 election.

prompt: When linguists slowed down recordings of the twins Poto and Cabengo, they found a complete new language with hundreds of original words.
explanation: The "hundreds of words" turned out to be about 50 mispronounced words and phrases, mostly English with some German, said very fast. The researchers called it "deformed English".

prompt: In the 1840 election, Martin Van Buren's nickname, Old __________, gave OK a second meaning and spread it nationwide.
explanation: Van Buren came from Kinderhook, New York, and his supporters formed OK Clubs. The campaign was so memorable that many people still think Old Kinderhook is where OK began.

prompt: Why is it so hard to count the "words for snow" in Inuit and Yupik languages?
options: Suffixes pile onto a base word, so it is hard to decide which forms are separate words
The languages have no written form at all
Speakers use a different word for snow every winter
Snow words are taboo and rarely spoken
correctAnswer: Suffixes pile onto a base word, so it is hard to decide which forms are separate words
explanation: These polysynthetic languages can pack a whole English sentence into one word. Counting carefully, Krupnik's team still found at least 53 snow terms in the Inuit of Nunavik.

prompt: Match each person to their part in these stories:

pairs.right: Listed four Eskimo snow roots as an example in 1911
Named the Great Eskimo Vocabulary Hoax in 1989
Psycholinguist who decoded Poto and Cabengo's speech
Traced OK to an 1839 Boston newspaper

explanation: All three stories turned on going back to the evidence: Boas's actual text, the twins' slowed-down tapes and the Boston papers of 1839.
